0: The first time you go to download a large model, the 7B, 32B, 128K and INT4 on the model page are easy to confuse: 7B says how big the model is, does 128K mean you can drop a whole book in, and why does INT4 let the model use less GPU memory?
1: Once you actually start using it you run into more: meeting notes that will not fit, long conversations that forget earlier context, answers with no basis, and a model whose results change when you switch to a different quantisation.
2: To judge whether a model suits the task at hand you first need to understand how text enters the model, how the model's abilities are trained, and why running it consumes memory and GPU memory.
3: This can be split into three threads. The first starts from the overall Transformer structure and then looks at Token, Embedding and Attention to explain how a piece of text enters and is processed by the model. The second is pre-training, instruction fine-tuning and post-training, explaining how the model's abilities are formed. The third is context length, KV Cache, quantisation and hardware, which decide whether the model can run stably on the target device.
4: This chapter distils the basics from the relevant earlier chapters. For model inference, for example, see chapters 6 and 7; for SFT see the ms-swift fine-tuning framework bundled with ModelScope described in chapter 9; for post-training, including preference alignment and reinforcement learning, see chapter 10. For domain-model applications and hallucination, see the RAG methods in chapter 13: using external knowledge both improves a large model's domain question answering and further reduces hallucination.
6: Transformer is the base architecture most large language models use today. Unlike earlier recurrent networks that process text in order, Transformer can compute several positions in parallel during training and input processing, and uses Attention to link different positions. The classic Transformer consists of an encoder and a decoder. Each Transformer layer usually contains Attention and a feed-forward network. The feed-forward network, also called FFN or MLP, applies a non-linear transformation to the vector at each position. The layer also uses residual connections and layer normalisation to help information pass through a deep network stably. Only by stacking many similar layers can the model gradually form complex text representations and generation ability. The overall Transformer architecture is shown below: on the left is the encoder and on the right the decoder. The N× in the figure means the same kind of module is stacked repeatedly; the actual number of layers varies with the architecture and parameter scale.
7: At inference, after the user enters some text the model processes it as follows: the model first uses a Tokenizer to split the raw text into Tokens and convert them into Token IDs; the Embedding layer then maps these discrete Token IDs into continuous vector representations and adds position information so the model knows the order of the Tokens in the sentence. These vectors then pass through many Transformer layers, where the Attention mechanism lets different Tokens attend to each other and exchange context, while the feed-forward network further processes the features at each position. After these layers the model obtains a combined representation of the current context, computes a probability distribution over the next Token from it, picks or samples the next Token, adds it to the context and repeats until the whole passage is generated.
8: The three parts of the original Transformer each have a different role:
9: Encoder-only structure: mainly responsible for understanding the input; it can refer to different positions in the input sequence at once, which suits classification, extraction and semantic representation tasks;
10: Decoder-only structure: mainly responsible for generating output; when generating the current position it can only look at what has already appeared;
11: Encoder-Decoder structure: understands the input first and then generates the output step by step, common in sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation and summarisation.
12: Modern large models do not necessarily use a complete encoder and decoder together. On top of that base, many Transformer variants have appeared: GPT-style generative models usually use a Decoder-only structure, BERT-style models mainly use Encoder-only, and T5-style models keep the Encoder-Decoder structure.
14: A token is the basic unit the model uses to read and generate text. It may be one Chinese character, a word, part of a word, a punctuation mark, or a space or special control marker. For example, the same sentence can produce different results in different Tokenizers:
15: Both results express the same sentence but the Token counts differ. What the model actually receives is the number for each Token, the Token ID. Taking meeting-minutes summarisation as an example, the model does not see a complete meeting record but a string of Token IDs. The meeting name, the speech content, the times, the punctuation and the output requirements all take Tokens; the summary, conclusions and action items the model generates take Tokens too. So the more detailed the required output from the same material, the less room may be left for the original record.
16: Splitting purely by character keeps the vocabulary small but makes sequences longer; splitting purely by whole words makes the vocabulary enormous and keeps running into new words, abbreviations and spelling variations. Large models usually use subword tokenisation, balancing between characters and whole words. BPE, WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece are all common methods.
18: Normally a model cannot do matrix arithmetic directly on text or images; the content must first be turned into numeric vectors. This process is called embedding. For text, the tokenizer first converts text into Token IDs and the Embedding layer then looks up the corresponding vector by ID. A single number in the vector usually has no intuitive meaning, but the whole vector can represent that Token's features inside the model. Take the Token for “meeting”: its Token ID could be some integer such as “15872”, and its representation, the Embedding, could be a vector like [0.12, -0.37, 0.08, ...]. Embeddings keep being adjusted during training, and Tokens appearing in similar contexts tend to develop similar features. Because model structures and training differ, the same word can form different representations after several Transformer layers depending on context.
19: When the model takes the semantic information from the input text it must know not only what the Token is but where it sits. With Token Embedding alone, for instance, “meeting postponed” and “postponed meeting” contain similar Tokens but express different meanings because the order differs. So the model also needs positional encoding or positional representation. The figure below takes BERT's input layer as an example.
20: As the representation used in BERT above shows, it combines Token Embedding, segment Embedding and position Embedding. Of course, different model structures and designs use different schemes. In a multimodal large model, images and audio must also be converted into vectors first. Images are usually cut into patches whose features a vision encoder extracts; audio is first turned into acoustic features and then handled by an audio encoder. Features from different modalities can only enter the vector space a large model can process after projection or a connection module. As shown below, the connection module fuses the image information with the semantic information.
22: Attention decides which parts of the input the current position should focus on. It computes how strongly the model's existing vector representations relate, not just which words are identical. For example, in “the project was delayed, and the report explained why it was not finished on time”, when processing the pronoun “it” the model must use the context to judge whether it more likely refers to “the project” or “the report”. When extracting owners from meeting notes, the model must likewise link the task description, the people's names and the sentences describing the division of work.
24: Each input vector goes through different transformations to form Query, Key and Value, usually written Q, K and V. The Attention formula can be simplified as:
26: Here Q is the information the current position is looking for, K is the feature by which each position can be matched, and V is the content to retrieve once matched. The model first compares Q and K to get relevance scores between the current position and the others; softmax then turns the scores into weights, and V is aggregated by those weights. In the formula, \(d_k\) is the dimension of the Key vector, and dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) adjusts the scale of the scores to make the computation more stable.
27: If Q, K and V come from the same sequence it is called self-attention, which links positions inside a sequence; if Q comes from one sequence while K and V come from another, it is called cross-attention. In an encoder-decoder translation model, for example, the decoder can read the source information the encoder provides through cross-attention.
28: For generative large models the current position may only refer to what has already appeared, so Attention also needs a causal mask that blocks later positions. Even with future Tokens masked, the number of relations full causal attention handles still grows roughly quadratically with sequence length. The generation stage must also keep the K and V of past Tokens, forming the KV Cache described later. As context grows, the compute and cache cost of Attention becomes more and more prominent, and the different structures below developed precisely around these problems.
30: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) was proposed in the 2017 Transformer paper “Attention Is All You Need” and later used in BERT and models such as Llama 2 7B and 13B. On top of a single attention computation it adds several parallel attention heads, letting the model extract context relations from different representation spaces.
31: In MHA each head has its own projection parameters producing Q, K and V, computes attention separately, and the head results are then concatenated and passed through a linear layer to form the output. As shown below, the left shows the computation of one scaled dot-product attention and the right runs it several times in parallel before fusing the results. The focus patterns of different heads are formed by training and together support tasks such as reference resolution, semantic association and long-range dependency.
32: MHA improves the model's ability to aggregate different kinds of information and is convenient for parallel computation during training. But when generating Token by Token each head must read its own past K and V. As layers, heads and context length grow, this cache and the associated data reads consume a lot of resources. Later improvements therefore first asked whether several Query heads could be kept while reducing the Key and Value heads that must be stored.
34: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) was proposed by Noam Shazeer in the 2019 paper “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need” and later used in models such as Falcon-7B. It targets the memory-bandwidth problem in decoding: every time the model generates a new Token it must read the existing KV Cache, and when that read is too large the generation speed is limited even if the compute units still have capacity.
35: MQA keeps several Query heads but makes them share one set of Key and Value. Different heads can still produce different queries, yet historical positions need only store one copy of K and V shared by all heads. The figure below shows one initialisation method for converting an existing MHA model into MQA: average the several Key projection matrices into one shared projection, and treat the Value projections the same way; after conversion the model must keep training to adapt to the new shared structure.
36: With this structure MQA markedly reduces the KV Cache and the data read per decoding step, freeing room for longer inputs or more concurrent requests. Falcon-7B, for example, has 71 Query heads but only 1 KV head. Against 71 KV structures with the same head dimension and precision, its theoretical KV cache is about one seventy-first. Sharing also constrains the representational capacity of K and V, so training and evaluation are needed to confirm how this efficiency gain affects task quality.
38: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) was systematically proposed by the Google Research team in the 2023 GQA paper and used in models such as Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B. It aims for a balance between MHA's multiple representation groups and MQA's low cache cost, avoiding a situation where every Query head must use the same K and V.
39: GQA divides the Query heads into groups, each sharing one set of Key and Value, with different groups keeping different K and V representations. As shown below, MHA gives every Query head its own K and V, MQA makes all Query heads share one set, and GQA shares within groups. When the number of groups equals the number of Query heads GQA is equivalent to MHA; with only one group it is equivalent to MQA.
40: Take Mistral 7B v0.1: it has 32 Query heads and 8 KV heads, so every 4 Query heads share one set of K and V. With the same head dimension and precision this cache is about a quarter of MHA's. For real deployment, less cache and fewer reads usually help concurrency and decoding efficiency; and because different groups keep their own K and V, GQA also preserves more representational space than the fully shared MQA. What is reduced here is the number of KV heads; the model can still compute attention over all the historical positions it is allowed to access.
42: Sliding Window Attention (SWA) comes from the local-attention idea in long-sequence modelling, and Mistral 7B v0.1 combines it with GQA. GQA reduces the KV heads stored per position, while SWA further limits the history each position attends to directly, lowering the compute and cache pressure of long text.
43: SWA gives each Token a fixed-size window and computes attention only over recent positions inside it. The figure below shows full causal attention on the left, sliding window attention in the middle, and on the right how information propagates backwards through the layers. Although one layer only reads a local range, the previous layer's Token representations already contain earlier context, so after several layers the model can indirectly use content outside the window.
44: Mistral 7B v0.1 uses a 4096-Token window and a rolling cache that overwrites the old K and V that have moved out of the window, keeping each layer's cache within a fixed range. For a 16K sequence with a 4096 window, the paper reports about twice the speed of the full-attention baseline after the corresponding kernel optimisation. This structure can control the resource growth of long text, but distant raw details must be passed through intermediate representations, so the local window size does not directly equal the context length the model can retrieve accurately.
46: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) was proposed by the DeepSeek team in DeepSeek-V2 and continues to be used in DeepSeek-V3. It also targets the oversized KV Cache but goes further in changing how the cache is stored: by learning a compact joint representation it reduces the data stored per Token while still letting several attention heads use that information.
47: Specifically, MLA first uses low-rank projection to jointly represent K and V as a lower-dimensional latent vector, and at inference mainly caches that vector plus a Key component that carries the rotary position information separately. Several Query heads can use this shared representation for matching and aggregation, and some projection matrices can be merged at inference, reducing explicit expansion into full K and V. The hatched areas in the figure below are what must be cached; you can see MLA moves the caching of multi-head K and V into the smaller latent representation on the right.
48: This design lets DeepSeek-V2 and V3 keep multi-head expressiveness while lowering the cache pressure of long-context generation. In the DeepSeek-V2 report, MLA's KV cache per Token is equivalent to a GQA with only 2.25 KV head groups. What it compresses is the representation dimension of each position; historical positions themselves are retained, so in full-attention mode the model must still read and match every historical entry. Reducing the number of entries actually involved in each computation requires sparse attention.
50: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) was proposed by the DeepSeek team and used in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and DeepSeek-V3.2. It adds a dynamic selection mechanism on top of MLA, solving the problem that in long contexts, even if each KV entry is already small, reading and computing over every historical entry is still expensive.
51: DSA first uses a lightweight Lightning Indexer to compute relevance scores between the current Query and historical Tokens, then takes the Top-k positions with the highest scores and hands them to the main Attention. The green part in the figure is the new indexing step: the Top-k Selector chooses the positions and the core Attention above reads the MLA cache for the selected positions. The indexer uses a smaller representation and fewer heads to do the filtering, so its cost is below running the full main Attention directly.
52: The configuration reported for DeepSeek-V3.2 is that each Query selects at most 2048 KV entries. As context grows the core Attention can still focus on this bounded range, clearly lowering the cost of processing long inputs and of subsequent generation. Historical entries not selected this time remain available to later Queries, so sparse selection mainly reduces this round's reads and computation rather than deleting all the cache in the same proportion. The indexer itself still has to process the historical candidates, so the actual overhead also depends on context length.
54: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) was proposed by the MiniMax team and used in MiniMax-M3. It targets efficiency in million-Token contexts and gives particular thought to making sparse attention suit GPU batch computation, not merely reducing the number of Tokens involved on paper.
55: MSA builds on GQA and has an indexing branch and a main branch. The indexing branch first computes Token-level relevance scores, then takes the highest score in each block as the block score, selecting Top-k historical blocks for each GQA group separately. The main branch then reads the Token-level K and V in the selected blocks that satisfy the causal condition, while keeping the local block it currently sits in. As shown below, the two Query groups on the right can form different selection ranges, while Query heads in the same group share the selection.
56: Organising access by block makes GPU data handling more regular, and grouped selection lets different groups keep different retrieval patterns. In a 1M-context test of a 109B-parameter experimental model, the paper reports that MSA's attention computation per Token is about 1/28.4 of GQA; with a dedicated kernel, processing input in the Prefill stage and generating Token by Token in the Decode stage on an H800 gained about 14.2x and 7.6x speedups respectively. This shows that the sparse algorithm and the compute kernel must be designed together for the reduced computation to translate fully into real speed.
58: Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) was proposed by the Qwen team and used in Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The model uses a hybrid structure of three Gated DeltaNet layers plus one QSA layer: the former handles sequences efficiently through state updates, the latter keeps direct retrieval of historical Tokens. QSA focuses on the problem that in long contexts the indexer itself also becomes costly.
59: So QSA first compresses the index Keys of several consecutive Tokens into micro-block representations by average pooling, computes relevance scores over the shorter micro-block sequence and selects the Top-k blocks. Selected blocks are then expanded back to the original Token positions for the core Attention to read the corresponding K and V; trailing Tokens that do not yet form a full block are kept as well. The left of the figure is the compressed indexing and the right the micro-block sparse Attention following the selection, with position indices passed between the two.
60: This reduces both the positions the main Attention visits and the sequence the indexer must scan. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reports that in a 1M-context kernel test, QSA improves Prefill and Decode speed over dense attention by about 7.6x and 4.9x respectively. When reading this structure, distinguish the index representation from the main Attention cache: QSA compresses the former to cut filtering cost, but after selection still reads Token-level KV, so it preserves fine-grained information in the selected region.
62: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) was proposed by the Moonshot AI team in Kimi Linear and is actually used in Kimi Linear's 48B-total, 3B-active-parameter model. It takes a linear-attention approach, writing historical information continuously into a fixed-size state to reduce the cost of repeatedly reading a long history at every generation step.
63: KDA introduces finer-grained gating on top of Gated DeltaNet. When a new Token arrives, the model first controls how much information in different channels of the old state is retained, then corrects the existing key-value associations through a Delta rule. This update can be understood as using the difference between the new input and what the current state predicts to adjust the information held in the state. Because the decay gate varies per channel, different parts can use different retention rates. The computation can also process a span of Tokens in blocks in parallel to improve GPU efficiency.
64: The figure above shows how Kimi Linear interleaves three KDA layers with one MLA layer. The KDA layers use a fixed-size state to lower long-sequence cost, while the MLA layer adds direct retrieval of specific historical positions, easing the limited capacity of a fixed state. In the paper's comparison under the same training scheme, this hybrid model reduces the KV Cache by up to 75% relative to a full MLA baseline and reaches up to about 6x decoding throughput at 1M context. These results correspond to Kimi Linear's hybrid architecture, not a uniform configuration across all Kimi models.
66: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) was proposed by the DeepSeek team in DeepSeek-V4 and used in DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Whereas MLA mainly compresses the KV representation of each Token, CSA goes further along the sequence direction to reduce the number of entries, converging the information of several Tokens into fewer KV entries and then doing sparse selection.
67: CSA first processes consecutive Tokens with a learnable Token-level compressor, combining overlapping information from adjacent blocks to form compressed KV. The Lightning Indexer then scores these compressed entries and selects the Top-k to take part in the main Attention. In the figure the compressor sits before indexing and selection, and the main Attention reads the compressed KV directly; there is also a sliding-window branch on the left that sends recent uncompressed Tokens into the computation, preserving local detail.
68: The CSA compression rate reported for DeepSeek-V4 is 4, i.e. the number of historical KV entries drops to about a quarter, from which some entries are then selected for the core Attention. So CSA lowers both the long-term cache volume and the historical content read and computed each time. QSA returns to the original Tokens after compressing the index, whereas CSA aggregates information directly on compressed entries, so it compresses the historical KV itself. This design requires the compressor to keep useful features and the local window to supply recent detail.
70: Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) was also proposed by the DeepSeek team in DeepSeek-V4 and is interleaved with CSA in the multi-layer structures of DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Flash. It uses stronger sequence compression so the model covers a wide range of history with a small cache, complementing CSA's selective reads.
71: HCA's compression rate is set to 128 in the report, far higher than CSA's 4. Several Tokens form one compressed entry through a learnable weighted aggregation, after which the current Query runs Attention over all causally visible compressed history with no Top-k filtering. As shown below, HCA keeps the compression branch and the local sliding-window branch but drops CSA's indexer and selector. The window supplies recent Token detail and the compressed history supplies wider context.
72: CSA and HCA are interleaved so DeepSeek-V4 can use historical representations of different granularities at once. In the report, at 1M context, DeepSeek-V4-Pro's per-Token inference FLOPs and KV Cache are about 27% and 10% of DeepSeek-V3.2's. That is the combined effect of hybrid Attention, low-precision computation and storage. For users, the point of such structures is that very long contexts become easier to run on limited hardware; whether a given model accurately extracts details from long material still depends on the compression scheme, the training process and the actual task.
73: From these designs you can see that Attention improvements do not follow a single direction. MHA, MQA and GQA mainly change the sharing between heads, MLA compresses the KV representation at each position, DSA, MSA and QSA reduce the positions the core Attention visits, KDA handles history through state updates, and CSA and HCA further compress historical entries. A model can combine several of them, so analysing resource needs requires knowing the layer count and cache form of each structure. Whichever structure is used, Attention only aggregates context; the model's overall ability is still formed together with Embedding, the feed-forward network and the training process.
75: The model structure determines how information is computed; the training process determines what the model ends up learning. Training a large model is usually split into stages. First comes pre-training, where the model learns language patterns, knowledge structures and basic reasoning from massive text and code and gains general ability. Next comes supervised fine-tuning (SFT), where many instruction-answer samples teach the model to understand what the user asks and to answer in the required task form. On that basis, preference optimisation or reinforcement learning further adjusts the model's behaviour according to human feedback or rules, so that answers better match expectations in usefulness, accuracy, style, safety and behavioural boundaries.
76: Pre-training is the stage in which the model forms its base abilities. It is trained repeatedly on large-scale text, code or multimodal data. For a Decoder-only language model (the GPT series, say), the usual training task is predicting the next Token from what precedes it and adjusting parameters when the prediction is wrong. After countless repetitions the model gradually learns language structure, ways of expression and statistical relations between concepts, forming the base representations and generation ability needed for question answering, summarisation, translation and code generation.
77: The knowledge a model learns in pre-training is distributed across a huge number of parameters, not a database you can query entry by entry. It can combine learned patterns to produce content that never appeared verbatim in the training data, and it can also combine related but not quite matching information into a plausible-looking wrong answer. Of course, more training data is not automatically better. Duplicated content, low-quality pages, wrong knowledge, private data and harmful content all affect the model. Before pre-training there is usually format parsing, deduplication, quality filtering, safety filtering and data mixing. Data scale determines how much content the model can encounter; data quality directly affects what it can learn from it.
79: After pre-training the model can continue text, but it will not necessarily complete tasks steadily as the user asks. If a user asks for three action items, a base model may keep expanding the question or ignore the specified format. Instruction fine-tuning continues training the model with examples made of an instruction and the expected answer; here is an example of instruction fine-tuning:
80: After training on different kinds of examples — question answering, summarisation, information extraction, code, tool calling and safe refusal — the model gradually learns to recognise user intent and follow output requirements. Instruction fine-tuning mainly teaches the model how to use the abilities it already has. It can add some knowledge but is not suited to solving every knowledge-update problem. Content that must be updated often, or that must cite sources, is better supplied at runtime through a knowledge base, retrieval or external tools.
82: Post-training is the collective name for a series of training and alignment steps done after pre-training. Instruction fine-tuning is usually part of post-training, and further SFT, preference optimisation and reinforcement learning may also appear at this stage. Instruction fine-tuning and post-training are therefore not two independent steps: the former is one specific method, the latter a stage containing several methods. These training approaches can be understood first through the following relationships:
87: Large-scale text, code and multimodal data
88: Let the model learn base patterns such as language and knowledge
91: Teach the model to output as the task requires
93: Better and worse answers to the same question
94: Make the model favour answers that match the preference
96: Prompts, model answers and reward signals
97: Keep adjusting the generation policy according to the reward
98: Following the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) framework used in InstructGPT, a classic post-training route has taken shape. RLHF usually uses human demonstration data for SFT first, then answer-ranking data to train a reward model, and finally uses the reward model's scores and PPO to optimise the language model's generation policy. The process is shown below.
99: The score a reward model gives represents a preference, not objective truth. If the preference data is too narrow, or the reward rules are poorly designed, the model may merely learn to please the scoring method.
100: Real models do not all follow exactly the same route. Some use SFT plus DPO, some use SFT, a reward model and PPO, and others add AI feedback, safety alignment, tool-use training and multi-turn dialogue data. The pre-training, instruction fine-tuning and post-training above explain how a model's abilities form. Once training is done, the questions users meet more often are how much content can be fed in at once, how much GPU memory running it needs, and which precision to choose on limited hardware.
102: Once training is complete the model enters actual inference and deployment. Context length determines how many Tokens one request can hold; the longer the context, the more material the model can read, but the Attention computation and KV Cache also grow, affecting inference speed and GPU memory needs. The context here is the system prompt, dialogue history, current input, file content, tool descriptions, tool return values and content the model has already generated in one request, which can be expressed as: context usage = system instruction + dialogue history + current input + attachment content + tool information + model output.
103: As mentioned above, a large model's context usage is not just what the user has typed but is made up of several parts: system instructions, the earlier dialogue history, the user's current input, relevant content in attachments, the information needed for tool calls and the output the model has already generated. All of it occupies the model's context window, so as the conversation grows, attachments multiply or tool information becomes complex, the context space left for later input and generation shrinks. When a model is labelled as supporting, say, 128K context, that usually means the order of magnitude of Tokens one request can process. Whether output is included and what the maximum single output is still depend on the model and the service interface limits. Usually, once the context is exceeded the platform may reject the request, truncate part of the content or automatically compress the history.
104: To improve a model's reasoning efficiency and answer quality on long documents, tidy the content before feeding it in: delete information irrelevant to the task, duplicated or of low value, and tell the model clearly which chapters, fields or questions to focus on, so it does not scatter its attention across a lot of irrelevant context. For material that is very long and hard to process in one go, split it by chapter, topic or fixed length, let the model extract, summarise or analyse each part, then aggregate and synthesise the partial results. For key conclusions, important figures or content needing further verification, also require the model to mark the corresponding source location, chapter or page, which makes later human checking and traceability easier and improves the accuracy, explainability and reliability of the whole process.
106: Generative models based on the Transformer architecture usually generate Tokens one by one; if every new Token recomputed the attention information of all previous Tokens it would repeat a great deal of work, so a caching mechanism, the KV Cache, is introduced. The KV Cache stores the Key and Value already computed at each layer, so generating the next Token only requires computing the new part, which speeds up generation. Each additional Token means every Transformer layer must store its K and V. The KV Cache therefore grows with context length, output length, concurrency and the number of layers.
107: For a common Decoder-only model, the cache usage of a single sequence can be understood with the following simplified formula, which can be written as:
108: \(\text{KV Cache usage} \approx 2 \times \text{number of layers} \times \text{number of Tokens} \times \text{number of KV heads} \times \text{dimension per head} \times \text{bytes per number} \)
109: The model weights take a relatively fixed amount once loaded, but the KV Cache varies with requests, so the same quantised model that runs fine on short Q&A may still run out of GPU memory with long documents or many concurrent users. For example, a server handling a single short meeting record may run normally, but if ten users upload long records at once the model must keep a KV Cache for each sequence and memory pressure rises sharply. This also explains why, even if the model file fits in GPU memory, the compute resources consumed keep changing as input length and concurrency grow. In deployment you can therefore shorten irrelevant context, cap the maximum generation length, lower concurrency, use paged caching, or pick models with GQA or MQA structures to reduce KV Cache pressure and improve the efficiency of the compute service.
111: A model file actually stores the current model structure and its parameters, which are essentially a set of numbers. From computer organisation, these parameters are usually a pile of 0s and 1s, and expressing the same value with a different number of bits both fixes the value range and constrains precision. During training, models usually compute in floating-point formats such as FP32, FP16 or BF16, i.e. using 32 or 16 bits of 0s and 1s per number. More bits increase both range and precision but also cost far more resources, so to reduce consumption further, quantisation was proposed: converting these multi-bit floating-point values into lower-precision representations such as 8-bit INT8 or 4-bit INT4, thereby cutting the model file and runtime resource usage. The table below shows the relevant characteristics of floating-point precisions:
120: Common training and high-precision inference format
123: Theoretical weight usage about half of 16-bit
126: Theoretical weight usage about a quarter of 16-bit
127: Real quantisation is not simply rounding every decimal but mapping a set of floating-point numbers onto a finite range and storing scale factors, zero points or grouping information. Common approaches include compressing only the weights, quantising both weights and activations, and post-training quantisation after training finishes. We need not worry too much about the numeric change quantisation causes, because in the end the model predicts the probability of each candidate Token as the next word, and selection depends more on ranking and normalised scores; so although quantisation loses precision, under strict control it can effectively balance the model's own generation quality.
128: When choosing a model you often need to judge whether GPU memory is enough. The 7B, 14B and 70B in model names usually mean roughly 7 billion, 14 billion and 70 billion parameters. Parameters are the numbers learned in training, distributed across Attention, the feed-forward network and Embedding modules.
129: The parameter count is not directly the model file size; the precision used for each parameter also matters. Counting model weights only, you can use the formula below:
130: \(weight usage ≈ parameter count × bytes per parameter \)
146: The numbers in the table are only the theoretical lower bound of the model weights. A quantised model must also store scale factors and similar information, and actual inference additionally needs the KV Cache, intermediate computation results, inference-framework workspace and caches for concurrent requests.
147: For example, the INT4 weights of a 14B model are theoretically about 7GB, but on an 8GB GPU that leaves almost no room for the KV Cache and runtime buffers. It may run with a short context and a single request, but long documents easily exhaust memory. 12GB or 16GB of GPU memory is more comfortable. 70B INT4 weights are about 35GB and generally need 48GB or more, so in deployment you can choose a larger-memory compute card, multiple cards, or hybrid inference using CPU memory.
149: A general large model has to cover a lot of knowledge and tasks and is not necessarily familiar with industry terminology, business processes and risk boundaries in specialised fields such as healthcare, finance, law and code. A domain model is usually built on a general base model by continuing training or adapting it with domain data and tasks, making it better suited to one field. It is not necessarily trained from scratch, and it is not just prompting the model to act as a professional. Common training and adaptation approaches include:
150: Continuing pre-training on unlabelled data such as domain literature, regulations and code repositories;
151: Domain instruction fine-tuning on data such as professional Q&A, information extraction and report generation;
152: Safety alignment using expert preferences, refusal rules and risk cases;
153: Connecting professional knowledge bases, databases and external tools to provide information that can be updated and traced.
154: Here you need to distinguish a domain model from a domain application. A domain model has been trained on professional data, so the expertise is written into its parameters; a domain application can use a general model directly and connect professional knowledge bases, rules and tools. Real systems often combine the two.
155: The legal Q&A system below first extracts keywords, then retrieves reference provisions from a regulation vector store, and finally a legal large model generates the answer together with the basis. This shows professional ability does not have to rely only on model parameters; external material is also an important part of a domain application.
156: Domain data does not equal domain reliability. Medical models must still check medical evidence and safety boundaries, legal models must check statutes and citations, financial models must check data currency and computation results, and code models must be verified by running and testing. High-risk tasks such as healthcare, law and finance should also keep professional approval.
158: When a model summarises meeting notes and invents a name where the original did not specify an owner, or when it extracts a contract and produces a specific figure where the original had no amount, those are hallucinations. A model hallucination is content a large model generates that is fluent and well structured yet inconsistent with the facts, the input material or a verifiable source. It can also appear as inventing policies, papers or web addresses that do not exist, getting people and dates wrong, or writing a discussion that never concluded as a settled conclusion.
159: A large model's core task is predicting the next Token from the context, and while generating it cannot verify whether each sentence is true. Hallucinations have many causes: pre-training data may contain wrong or outdated information; the user's question may lack key conditions; evidence in long text may be ignored or truncated. If post-training designs a reward function that favours complete, fluent answers, the model may also keep generating when it lacks grounds.
161: Model hallucinations are varied and can usually be grouped into factual, citation, input, reasoning and tool hallucinations; the detailed types and typical manifestations are shown in the table below:
165: Names, dates, figures and events that do not match reality
167: Inventing papers, statutes, links or sources
169: Generating conclusions and fields that do not appear in the original material
171: An error in the intermediate derivation, stated with great confidence
173: Claiming a file was read or an interface was called when it was not
174: Besides general models, domain models obtained through training also hallucinate. Usually professional data improves domain performance but cannot guarantee every answer is accurate. Knowledge-base retrieval cannot fully solve hallucination either: if the retrieved material is irrelevant, outdated or itself wrong, the model may still reach a wrong conclusion and hallucinate further.
176: Hallucination is a fairly common problem in current applications, and merely adding “do not make things up” or “please make sure the answer is accurate” to the prompt usually cannot remove the risk at the root. The model is still essentially predicting the most likely content from the context, so when the input is insufficient, the material conflicts or the question goes beyond the model's reliable knowledge, it may still produce an answer that looks plausible but is not accurate. Reducing hallucination therefore relies more on a whole set of input constraints, external verification and human review.
177: First, give the model material that is clear, relevant and mutually consistent, reducing the interference of irrelevant and conflicting information. For key content such as facts, figures, policy clauses and experimental results, require the model to mark the corresponding source, chapter, page or original location, so answers are traceable and easy to verify later. For fast-changing knowledge such as news, policy, prices, regulations and product specifications, do not rely only on the model's internal memory but fetch the latest information through search engines, knowledge bases, databases, APIs or other external tools and let the model analyse based on that reliable material.
178: Second, when the original material really lacks some information, require the model to mark it explicitly as “to be confirmed”, “not provided in the original” or “cannot be judged from the available material” rather than filling it in from experience. For content suited to structured checking, such as dates, amounts, ID numbers, statistics, formulas and code execution results, you can also bring in a program to verify automatically, for example checking value ranges, field formats, computation results and whether code actually runs, so the model does not rely on language alone to produce the result.
179: In addition, for important conclusions, especially those affecting business decisions, project acceptance or user rights, keep a human review step. Fluent language and apparently complete logic do not guarantee the facts are right, so “it sounds true” must not be equated with “it is true”. In high-risk scenarios such as healthcare, law, finance and safety production, be even clearer that the model is only an aid and the final conclusion must be reviewed and confirmed by professionals with the relevant qualifications and experience.
180: So the core idea for reducing hallucination is not to demand that the model “always answer” but to teach it to stop sensibly when reliable grounds are missing. When the available information cannot support a conclusion, the most appropriate behaviour may be to state clearly “which key materials are missing” and “which conclusions cannot be confirmed for now”, and further tell the user what data, documents or evidence to supply. Compared with continuing to generate a seemingly complete answer without grounds, this is usually more reliable and better suited to real business applications.
